::: {#explain .lx-sec}

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="merit-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Supply stack</dt><dd>All offers lined up from cheapest to dearest, each as wide as its MW and as high as its offer. Here each offer starts equal to the plant's running cost.</dd>
<dt>Clearing price</dt><dd>The offer of the marginal plant, the one that serves the last MW of demand; every running plant is paid it.</dd>
<dt>Gas sets the price, often</dt><dd>When a gas plant is marginal, each $1 per MMBtu (million British thermal units) of gas adds its <span class="lx-term" data-term="heat-rate">heat rate</span> in dollars to every MWh that hour.</dd>
<dt>More wind, lower prices</dt><dd>Wind offers about $0, so more wind cuts the output needed from dearer plants. The price falls when a cheaper offer becomes the marginal one.</dd>
<dt>Below zero</dt><dd>The price turns negative only when the last plant needed offers below $0: it earns a credit per MWh, or would rather pay than stop and restart.</dd>
<dt>An optimization in disguise</dt><dd>The stack is the cheapest way to meet demand. While the marginal plant has room, the price is the cost of one more MWh: the shadow price of supply equals demand.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Economic dispatch as a linear program</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

For one hour, with $p_g$ the output of plant $g$ in MW, $c_g$ its offer in \$/MWh, $\bar P_g$ what it can make this hour and $D$ the demand:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{p}\;\; & \textstyle\sum_g c_g\, p_g \\
\text{subject to}\;\; & \textstyle\sum_g p_g = D \quad (\lambda)\\
& 0 \le p_g \le \bar P_g \quad (\text{each } g).
\end{aligned}
$$

Every term is linear, so this is a [linear program]{.lx-term term="linear-program"}. For one hour, 1 MW of output makes 1 MWh, so offer × MW is dollars.

- **The data at 19:00.** $c = (0, 0, 10, 40, 100)$, $\bar P = (72, 14, 100, 150, 100)$ and $D = 331$.
- **The answer.** $p = (72, 14, 100, 145, 0)$, at a running cost of $100 \times 10 + 145 \times 40 = \$6{,}800$.
- **One more MWh.** With $D = 332$ the cost is \$6,840. The [shadow price]{.lx-term term="shadow-price"} $\lambda$ of the balance rule is \$40 per MWh, the clearing price.
- **At a block edge.** At $D = 336$ the combined-cycle plant is full, so the 337th MWh comes from the peaker and adds \$100.
- **Over a day.** [Lesson 0](00-grid-operator.html) wrote the same problem over 24 hours with a ramp limit, which ties the hours together.

```{=html}
<div id="merit-solver" class="lx-merit-solver"><p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, a button here hands this hour to the HiGHS solver in your browser.</p></div>
```

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Prices over a day and a network, and where this one-hour picture stops</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><a href="m01-dispatch-to-lmp.html">M1</a> (Modeler tier) builds a 24-hour dispatch linear program with ramps, adds a three-bus network, fills a line and reads one price per bus from the solver.</li>
<li>With on/off decisions and start-up costs (<a href="m02-unit-commitment.html">M2</a>), the energy price may not cover a running plant's start-up costs; some markets then add side payments, called uplift.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this one-hour stack leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Offers are not always costs: sellers can add a mark-up, and market monitors watch for it.</li>
<li>Start-up costs, minimum outputs and ramp limits, which link one hour to the next.</li>
<li>Reserves held back for surprises (lesson 3), and the network, which the last step only hints at.</li>
<li>Many markets clear a day ahead and again in real time, and cap prices in shortages.</li>
<li>Demand that answers the price, such as batteries and flexible users (<a href="09-storage.html">lesson 9</a>, and A3, upcoming).</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="m8-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="paid" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Each plant is paid the price it offered.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In a uniform-price market every running plant is paid the clearing price: at 19:00 the solar farm offers $0.00 and is paid $40.00.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="average" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The wholesale price is the average cost of the plants that run.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It is the offer of the last plant needed, the marginal plant, not an average.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="wind" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “More wind can lower the price of every MWh in that hour.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. At 19:00 a 475 MW wind farm pushes the combined-cycle plant out of the stack, and the price falls from $40.00 to $10.00.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="negative" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A negative price means the grid has failed.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It means the last plant needed would pay to keep running; it signals more power in that place than can be used right then.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="m8">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="stack" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">Offers, in $/MWh: wind 80 MW at $0, a 100 MW plant at $10, a 150 MW plant at $40 and a 100 MW plant at $100. Demand is 250 MW. What is the clearing price?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$0/MWh</li><li data-value="b">$10/MWh</li><li data-value="c">$40/MWh</li><li data-value="d">$100/MWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$40/MWh: the first two offers cover 180 MW, so the $40 plant serves the last 70 MW and sets the price.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="gas" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">A combined-cycle plant that burns 6 MMBtu per MWh is marginal. Gas rises from $6 to $8 per MMBtu. How much does the price rise?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$2 per MWh</li><li data-value="b">$6 per MWh</li><li data-value="c">$12 per MWh</li><li data-value="d">$48 per MWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$12 per MWh: 6 MMBtu × $2 more per MMBtu.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::

<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>West Texas, as EIA reported it (<a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=16831">June 2014</a>):</p>
<ol>
<li>Wind farms far from the cities filled the lines out of the region: the grid was <span class="lx-term" data-term="congestion">congested</span>.</li>
<li>Local prices fell below zero, and wind was curtailed.</li>
<li>A major grid expansion added more than 3,500 miles of lines by the end of 2013.</li>
<li>Curtailments and negative prices became less frequent.</li>
</ol>
<p>Builds on <a href="00-grid-operator.html">lesson 0</a> (cheapest first) and <a href="07-cost.html">lesson 7</a> (what a plant must earn back).</p>
